abstract: |
  The murderer at the door is Benjamin Constant's example, introduced in 1797 to illustrate a theory on which the essence of a principle is not generality but fixity: a principle is a rule people can count on, as against the arbitrary. By that standard Constant's own resolution of the case, that no one has a right to a truth that harms others, fails, for reasons already noticed by his critics and by Kant: a duty keyed to harm makes each speaker judge of circumstances. But the pamphlet shows the case Constant had in mind, the proscribed man seeking asylum, and a neglected note of 1815 states the principle that case needed: "when pretended laws demand the truth of us only to proscribe us, we do not owe them the truth." That principle is keyed not to harm but to the title of the demand; it meets both Constant's standard and Kant's distinction between harming and wronging; and it shows, against the leading recent study, that the case concerns the state. What remains between Constant and Kant is a disagreement about authority, not about principles.

# Constant's example {#sec-intro}

The example now called "the murderer at the door" is not Kant's. In the eighth chapter of *Des réactions politiques*, a pamphlet signed at Hérivaux on 10 germinal year V (30 March 1797), Benjamin Constant wrote that "a German philosopher" goes so far as to claim "that towards assassins who asked you whether your friend, whom they are pursuing, has not taken refuge in your house, a lie would be a crime" [@Constant1797, 74].^[Translations from Constant and Kant are mine. After this note, @Constant1797 is cited by page alone; Kant is cited by volume and page of the Akademie edition [@KantAA], the *Critique of Pure Reason* by B-pagination.] Kant read the passage in Carl Friedrich Cramer's German translation, admitted in a note that he had said something of the kind (8:425), and replied in September in "On a Supposed Right to Lie from Love of Humanity". The reply became one of the most discussed short texts in moral philosophy, and Constant became its foil.

He has usually been cast in one of two parts. In one he is the voice of expediency, for whom a principle yields when following it is dangerous; the title of @Benton1982, "Political Expediency and Lying", names the part. In the other, which is more careful, he restates an "eighteenth-century commonplace": that a would-be murderer forfeits his right to the truth [@Timmermann2025, 96; cf. 98–100]. That is Jens Timmermann's reading in the first monograph on the exchange, which also holds that Constant "is not talking about the state" and that neither philosopher "is concerned with sincerity in the public sphere" [-@Timmermann2025, 95–96 nn. 59–60].

I argue that both parts miss what is distinctive in Constant, and that Timmermann's reading of the case as non-political is mistaken. Constant introduces the example to illustrate a theory of what principles are, on which a principle's essence is its *fixity*, not its generality, and its point is to protect against the arbitrary (@sec-principles). By that standard his 1797 resolution fails. It is keyed not to the questioner's forfeiture but to harm, and a duty so keyed is one nobody can count on; critics and Kant himself have noticed the defect, and Constant's theory explains why it is fatal by his own lights (@sec-example). The pamphlet shows what case Constant had in mind, the proscribed man seeking asylum, and a note of 1815, so far as I know never connected with the exchange, states the principle that case needed, keyed to the title of whoever demands the truth: "when pretended laws demand the truth of us only to proscribe us, we do not owe them the truth" (@sec-needed). That principle meets Constant's standard and Kant's distinction between harming and wronging, and its paradigm is a demand made by the state. What then remains between Constant and Kant is a disagreement about authority (@sec-remains).

# What a principle is {#sec-principles}

*Des réactions politiques* defends the republican constitution of year III against the reactions that followed the Terror: the reaction against the Terror's crimes, which became a counter-terror, and the reaction against the ideas in whose name the crimes were committed. Its seventh to ninth chapters defend principles against those who exaggerate them until they become inapplicable and those who conclude from the excesses that principles are useless; Burke is named in chapter IX for holding that axioms "metaphysically true" can be "politically false" (81).

Chapter VIII, "Des principes", begins with a definition:

> A principle is the general result of a certain number of particular facts. Whenever the set of these facts undergoes some change, the principle that resulted from it is modified; but then this modification itself becomes a principle. (66)

Every combination of existences or events leads to a result, "and this result is always the same, whenever the combinations are the same" (66). Such a result "is general only in relation to the combinations from which it results. It is therefore general only in a relative and not an absolute way. This distinction is of great importance" (66). There are universal principles, because some data are present in all combinations, but to them must be added principles "resulting from each particular combination" (67). Those who call general principles inapplicable mean only that the intermediate principle a combination requires has not been found: "one of the links of the chain" is lost, but the chain exists (67). Then the central claim:

> Secondary principles are just as immutable as first principles. Each interruption of the great chain has only one link to fill it. … Each circumstance calls only for the principle proper to it, for the essence of a principle is not to be general, nor applicable to many cases, but to be fixed; and this quality so far makes up its essence that all its utility resides in it. (67–68)

Two properties are distinguished. A principle's *generality* is its breadth, the range of cases it covers. Its *fixity* has two aspects. One is formal: like combinations, like results. The other is practical: a fixed principle can be relied on, which is why "all its utility" lies in fixity. Chapter IX, "De l'arbitraire", makes the practical aspect explicit. The arbitrary is "the absence of rules, of limits, of definitions, in a word the absence of all that is precise" (80), and morality is "an assemblage of rules on which individuals must be able to count mutually in their social relations" (82). Without principles "there is nothing fixed: only circumstances remain, and each person is judge of the circumstances"; where "everything is wavering, no fulcrum is possible" (78).

Kant had terms for the first contrast. Experience gives its judgements "only assumed and comparative universality (through induction)", while strict universality, which "allows no exception as possible", marks the a priori (B3–4). Constant's principles, "general results" of facts, are comparatively universal in Kant's sense, and he says so. What he denies is that it matters. A principle's authority comes neither from its breadth nor from its source but from the fixed connection between a type of combination and a result. In later terms he separates universality from generality, as Hare did when he wrote that "generality is the opposite of specificity, whereas universalizability is compatible with specificity" [@Hare1981, 41]. But the period's own contrast is the better guide, and Kant states it in his last sentence on Constant: intermediate principles may contain "the closer determination [*nähere Bestimmung*] of their application to cases", but "never exceptions" (8:430). Both men accept that criterion. The dispute is over what falls on each side of it.

The chapter's model is political. That "no man can be bound except by laws to whose formation he has contributed" is a universal principle; in a large society it is applied through an intermediate principle, that individuals may contribute "either in person or through their representatives" (72). Someone who applied the first principle to a large society without the second would overthrow it, but that would prove "nothing against the principle" (72). Kant calls Constant's remark on inapplicable principles "well thought and at the same time correct" (8:427) and restates the political example as an axiom, a postulate and a problem solved by the representative system (8:429). The agreement is not surprising, if chapter VIII answers Kant's essay of 1793 on theory and practice, as Hinz has argued [@Timmermann2025, 43 n. 16]; there Kant had written that when theory is of little use in practice "it was not the fault of the theory, but that there was not enough theory" (8:275).

What Constant took to be new was a method. An intermediate principle is found by *defining* the principle that seems inapplicable, "surveying its whole circumference", until we find "the link that unites it to another principle" (74–75): "It is an idea perhaps new, but which seems to me infinitely important, that every principle contains, either in itself or in its relation to another principle, its means of application" (77). Here Kant and Constant part, though neither says so. In 1793 Kant had insisted that between a rule and its application there must be an act of judgement for which rules cannot always be given, "because that would go on to infinity" (8:275). Constant's method tries to do without that act; as Timmermann puts it, "personal judgement has no role to play because the scope of one principle is limited by another" [-@Timmermann2025, 94 n. 56]. The chain of principles, completed by definition, is to leave nothing to judgement, and so nothing to the arbitrary. That is the standard by which Constant's resolution of his example should be measured.

# The example and its key {#sec-example}

Morality, Constant says, is "a science much more advanced than politics", because the need for it is daily and its intermediate principles are better known; yet its abstract principles, cut off from those intermediate principles, would disorder social relations as badly as abstract political principles disorder civil ones (73). Then the example:

> The moral principle, for example, that telling the truth is a duty, if it were taken in an absolute and isolated way, would make all society impossible. We have the proof of this in the very direct consequences that a German philosopher has drawn from this principle, who goes so far as to claim that towards assassins who asked you whether your friend, whom they are pursuing, has not taken refuge in your house, a lie would be a crime. (74)

The questioners are plural, and the person they pursue has "taken refuge" in your house. There is no stipulation that you must answer yes or no, or that a lie might misfire; those are Kant's (8:426–427), made to a translation in which the assassins had become "a murderer" (8:425).^[Timmermann notes the plural and the absence of the binary restriction [-@Timmermann2025, 77 n. 1, 78], and argues that Kant's "unjust compulsion" is the pursuer's threat of violence (81).]

The case is set up as a dilemma. Taken in isolation, the principle "is inapplicable. It would destroy society. But if you reject it, society will be no less destroyed, for all the foundations of morality will be overturned" (75). Constant shares Kant's premise that truthfulness is a foundation of social life. The way out is definition:

> Telling the truth is a duty. What is a duty? The idea of duty is inseparable from that of rights: a duty is what, in one being, corresponds to the rights of another. Where there are no rights, there are no duties. Telling the truth is therefore a duty only towards those who have a right to the truth. But no man has a right to a truth that harms others. (75–76)

"There, it seems to me, is the principle become applicable" (76). The man who, "struck by the inconveniences of the principle", declaimed against abstractions instead of defining it "would have thrown everything into the arbitrary"; by defining it "we have found the precise modification of the principle of truth, which excludes all arbitrariness and all uncertainty" (76–77).

By Constant's lights this is not an exception. When the facts change, "this modification itself becomes a principle" (66), and the restricted duty is such a modification, "just as immutable" as the duty it restricts. @Zupancic1993 [179] is right that the word "exception" does not appear. The question Constant's theory makes pressing is whether the modification is *fixed*, and that depends on what it is keyed to.

It is keyed to harm. The clause does not say that those who would use the truth for a crime lose their right to it, or that assassins are owed nothing. It says that no one has a right to a truth "qui nuit à autrui", that harms someone other than the questioner. The assassins drop out of the statement of the principle; what decides is the truth's effect on the friend. Timmermann registers this, glossing the clause as denying a right to the truth to those whose "knowing and acting on this truth will harm another" [-@Timmermann2025, 100], but he describes the result as forfeiture, the would-be murderer losing a right by his intent. Forfeiture would make the case turn on the questioner. Constant's 1797 clause makes it turn on consequences.

A clause so keyed fails Constant's standard in two ways. The first is that it is not precise. As Kettner and Annen have pointed out, it releases too much: a witness whose truthful testimony will convict the accused tells a truth that harms another, so by the clause the court has no right to it [@Timmermann2025, 100 n. 11]. Annen adds that Constant was proud of the precision of his argument (ibid.). For Constant this is worse than a counterexample. To exclude the witness he would need an exception to his intermediate principle, the very structure his method was meant to replace, or another modification found by further definition, whose key he does not supply.

The second failure goes to fixity itself. A truth harms others or not depending on what others then do. Kant's own variation makes the point: the friend may have slipped out, so that the lie sends the murderer to meet him (8:427). Michaelis had rejected harm-based definitions of the lie on the same ground, "that I can never be certain whether this or that untruth may not be very harmful to another", and Timmermann draws the moral that on such a definition "we can never know in advance whether we are lying or merely uttering a falsified statement" [-@Timmermann2025, 169]. For Constant the moral is sharper. A duty keyed to harm can be applied only by forecasting, so each speaker decides, case by case, whether the truth he is asked for will harm someone: "only circumstances remain, and each person is judge of the circumstances" (78). That is Constant's definition of the arbitrary. Those who deal with someone bound only by his clause cannot count on what he says, since he will lie whenever he judges the truth harmful, and the clause fails the test of chapter IX. It offers no fulcrum.

Kant names the missing key. The "French philosopher", he says, confused "the action by which someone harms (*nocet*) another by telling the truth, the admission of which he cannot avoid, with that by which he wrongs (*laedit*) him" (8:428). The witness harms the accused without wronging him. Campagna's proposed repair, which adds that the person harmed must himself intend harm to others, keeps the key on harm, and so, as Timmermann observes, leads toward a negative utilitarianism [-@Timmermann2025, 100 n. 11]. Constant would not have accepted that destination; his theory asks for a modification that is fixed. What would such a modification look like?

# The principle the case needed {#sec-needed}

Constant's example is spare, but the pamphlet around it is not. Its first chapter describes leaders of the reaction who incited their followers "to the assassination of their accomplices" and made "national vengeance illegal and atrocious" (6). Chapter VII warns that if the royalists triumphed "proscription would be without end and without limits" (50), and calls on the friends of liberty to defend men "exalted in their opinions but not stained by crimes", whom some would make "a proscribed and terrible race, which would have no asylum on earth but beneath the ruins of the social order" (56–57). Chapter IX says that the revolutionary government of the Terror "offered no protective form, no fixed law, nothing precise, determined, nothing therefore that could guarantee"; "founded on no law", its agents had massacred "without judgement or by arbitrary judgements", and fell in turn: "they had put outside the law, and they were put outside the law" (90–91).

In this pamphlet, a friend who has taken refuge in your house from those pursuing him is the *proscrit* seeking asylum, and his pursuers are the agents of proscription, whether they carry a decree of outlawry or belong to the bands of the reaction. Others have placed the example in the Revolution. Holmes, quoted by Wood, has Constant's view formed where "the line separating police officials from murderers was not necessarily well-defined" [@Wood2011; @Holmes1984], and @Troitsky2016 [88 n. 56] imagines the caller as a Jacobin searching for a Girondin. Timmermann replies that Constant files truthfulness under morals, not politics, and uses the case to show that moral science is the more advanced [-@Timmermann2025, 95–96 and nn. 59–60]. That is true of what chapter VIII says. But it shows only that the 1797 clause was formulated as a moral principle without reference to authority, and the last section showed that the clause fails. What the pamphlet adds is a vocabulary in which the case could be stated, and that vocabulary concerns law: the Terror was arbitrary because it rested on no law, so its decrees had the form of law without the substance. Constant's 1797 clause does not use this vocabulary. Eighteen years later he did.

Chapter XVII of the *Principes de politique* of 1815 discusses Rousseau's civil profession of faith, whose articles the sovereign may fix and whose unbelievers he may banish, not as impious but as unsociable. A footnote reports Rousseau's addition, that whoever has publicly acknowledged the dogmas and behaves as if he did not believe them is to be punished with death: "he has committed the greatest of crimes, he has lied before the laws".^[*Du contrat social* IV.8, as paraphrased in Constant's note. I cite the 1815 text from Laboulaye's edition [@Constant1872], which reprints the *Principes* as the first part of the *Cours de politique constitutionnelle*.] Constant replies:

> But he who has the misfortune not to believe these dogmas cannot avow his doubts without exposing himself to banishment; and if his affections hold him back, if he has a family, a wife, children whom he hesitates to leave to rush into exile, is it not you, you alone, who force him to what you call the greatest of crimes, to lying before the laws? I will say, moreover, that in this circumstance this lie seems to me far from being a crime. *Quand de prétendues lois n'exigent de nous la vérité que pour nous proscrire, nous ne leur devons pas la vérité*: when pretended laws demand the truth of us only to proscribe us, we do not owe them the truth. [@Constant1872, 128–129 n. 1]

The text the note annotates asks what it matters that the sovereign does not strike me as impious if he strikes me as unsociable, or that authority abstains from theology "if it loses itself in a hypothetical morality, no less subtle, no less foreign to its natural jurisdiction" (129).

Two cautions. I know of no evidence that Constant had the 1797 exchange in mind, and the case is a demanded profession of belief, not a hunted friend. The claim is structural: here Constant states, in the language of owed truth he used in 1797, a principle with the key the 1797 clause lacked. Four features show it.

First, the principle is keyed to wrong. The demand is made "only to proscribe us", and proscription is the paradigm wrong of Constant's politics. Nothing in the note turns on the truth's effects. A genuine law may demand truth that harms, as the court demands it of the witness.

Second, it is keyed to the title of the demand. The laws are *prétendues*, laws in name only, and "we do not owe them" the truth. The 1797 correlation survives, since a duty is owed to those with a right, but the right now belongs to authority acting within its jurisdiction, and a law that legislates belief is "foreign to its natural jurisdiction". On this reading the right to the truth is not a claim on propositions, which was Kant's complaint about the phrase: truth is not "a possession" granted to one and refused to another (8:428). It is the standing to demand an answer. Constant's theory of sovereignty supplies the criterion for that standing: sovereignty "exists only in a limited and relative way", and "at the point where independence and individual existence begin, the jurisdiction of this sovereignty stops" [@Constant1872, 9].

Third, it covers the 1797 case. Assassins who ask where your friend is so as to kill him demand the truth only in order to wrong him, and they lack even the pretence of law. The historical case behind the example, agents executing a decree of outlawry, falls under the note's wording directly.

Fourth, the paradigm is a statement demanded by the state on pain of punishment, a "lie before the laws". Timmermann is right that the 1797 chapter does not talk about the state. The principle the case needed does.

Does it meet Constant's standard? Whether a demand comes from law within its jurisdiction, and whether its purpose is proscription, are not forecasts of what others will do. They are features of the demand, settled by public rules about what authority may require, the rules the whole of the 1815 *Principes* sets out to state. The court and its witness, and the declarations on which contracts rest, keep the reliance Kant cares about. The principle withholds truthfulness only from those who demand it in order to proscribe, and everyone can know in advance which demands those are. It also passes Kant's distinction. The witness harms the accused without wronging him; the man who answers the proscriber lends himself to a wrong.

The principle is closer to Kant than either man knew. Kant agrees that the questioner is not wronged: "I do no wrong to him who unjustly compels me to a statement if I falsify it" (8:426). Timmermann considers two explanations, that the pursuer has forfeited a right to the truth or that he never had one, and prefers the second, following Weinrib: rights to a truthful answer exist only in particular juridical relations, such as contract, and do not depend on "the behaviour, character or intentions of the person who asks the question" [-@Timmermann2025, 118–120]. That is the structure of Constant's 1815 principle. A right to the truth is a title, conferred by a relation of right; legitimate law within its jurisdiction has it, and neither pretended laws nor assassins do. On this point Constant's considered view and the best reading of Kant's coincide, and neither rests on forfeiture.

# What remains {#sec-remains}

What divides them is Kant's further claim. Although the questioner is not wronged, the lie wrongs "humanity in general", because it makes statements in general unbelievable and "renders the source of right unusable" (8:426). Constant's reply is available from the note: a pretended law is not a source of right, so truthfulness towards it does not sustain the institution of declarations, any more than a decree of outlawry sustains the institution of justice. Kant cannot accept this reply, and the reason lies in his theory of authority, not in his theory of principles.

In the *Doctrine of Right*, published earlier in 1797, the subject owes obedience to "the legislative power now existing, whatever its origin may be" (6:319). He may oppose its injustices with "complaints (*gravamina*), but no resistance" (6:319), and there can be no lawful resistance, since the question "who is to be judge in this dispute between people and sovereign" has no answer except one that makes the people judge in its own cause (6:320). On that view there is no category of pretended laws for a subject to identify: the judgement Constant's principle calls for is one the subject is not entitled to make. @Troitsky2016 links Kant's ban on lying with his ban on resistance. On the reading defended here the link runs through Constant's own principle, which turns on exactly the judgement of title that Kant withholds from subjects.

The contrast is sharp at one point. Kant says the subject must obey "whatever its origin may be". Constant, in the chapter that states the limits of sovereignty, says that when any authority commits acts beyond its competence, "it matters little from what source it claims to derive" [@Constant1872, 9]. Both deny that origin settles the question, to opposite effect. For Kant origin cannot undo the duty to obey; for Constant origin cannot confer a title that the scope of the act denies.

Constant's view of who judges also changed, in a direction that concedes something to Kant. In 1797, definition was to yield a modification "which excludes all arbitrariness". In 1815, discussing subordinate agents who execute illegal orders, Constant argued that passive obedience cannot be maintained without restriction, but admitted: "Nor can you indicate with precision each circumstance in which obedience ceases to be a duty and becomes a crime." It is "impossible … to regulate everything, to write everything", and "whatever one does, there always remains in human affairs something discretionary" [@Constant1872, 94–95]. His answer was institutional. The residual judgement goes to juries, who exercise it once and have no permanent interest in power. That concedes Kant's point of 1793, that applying rules needs a judgement rules cannot exhaust (8:275), while placing the judgement where it is least arbitrary.

At the door there is no jury. But the judgement the 1815 principle requires is not the one the 1797 clause required. It is not a forecast of harm, made by each speaker for each truth. It is a judgement about whether a demand has the title of law, of a kind Constant thought citizens must be able to make if limited sovereignty is to mean anything, and of a kind Kant thought they must not make if there is to be a civil condition at all.

That is where centring Constant leaves the murderer at the door. The case Kant made famous simplifies the one Constant described: a lone murderer in place of the agents of proscription, a forced yes or no in place of a refuge. Constant's own 1797 answer fails by his own standard, as his critics and in effect Kant showed. But the theory in which he set it was not expediency. It was a theory of principles as fixed rules against the arbitrary, and that theory, together with his politics of limited sovereignty, yields a principle that meets both his standard and Kant's distinction between harming and wronging. Constant's question was never simply whether one may lie to save a friend. It was whether truth is owed to power that has exceeded its jurisdiction.
